body_markdown:
In the last six years, Ford has been content to change its cash-cow F-150 in ways that are evolutionary, not revolutionary. The updates for the 2027 model year are similarly incremental, concentrated on the higher-end trims and on BlueCruise, with one major exception.


As expected, the base engine has changed: The 325-hp, twin-turbo 2.7-liter EcoBoost is out, and the twin-turbo, 3.0-liter EcoBoost is in. Yes, this is the same engine in the Explorer ST and[Tremor](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2026-ford-explorer-tremor-v-6-another-class-of-one/) , where it makes 400 hp and 415 lb-ft of torque, and in the[Raptor versions](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2024-ford-ranger-raptor-everything-you-want-in-a-pickup-and-less/) of the Bronco and Ranger, where it makes even more. In the F-150, however, the three-liter makes exactly as much power and torque as the 2.7: 325 hp and 400 lb-ft of torque. However, peak torque arrives earlier, at 2250 rpm vs 3500. The engines share a “core architecture,” says Ford, though the 3.0 runs slightly higher compression (10.5:1 vs 10.1:1) and uses only direct injection.

As for the higher-trim models, the posh ones get more cylinders while the off-road ones get more affordable. Well, sort of: The Tremor and the Raptor are each available in a new, “entry-level” configuration. The entry-level Tremor is based on the STX, which is super confusing, because the regular Tremor remains *its own distinct trim* . At least the entry-level Tremor doesn’t hide its origins: It has an STX steering wheel, manual rather than dual-zone air conditioning, no heated seats, a stereo with six speakers instead of eight, no off-road running boards, and fixed rear glass. You’ll pay $62,400 for the STX-based Tremor, about $5300 less than the current, regular Tremor.


The entry-level Raptor is a Raptor with all the off-road kit but with fewer creature comforts. A list of things that the entry-level version does not have: Heads-up display, fog lamps, 2kW Pro Power Onboard, Mobile Office Package, power passenger seat, under-seat storage, and a 14-speaker sound system. It’s like the Porsche Carrera T of the F-150 range! The entry-level 2027 Raptor costs $77,800, or about $4000 lower than the current Raptor.


The two poshest F-150s, the[King Ranch](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/sun-snakes-cattle-and-ford-trucks-have-been-part-of-king-ranch-for-decades/) and the Platinum, don’t get additional trims, but they do, once again, get the 5.0-liter V-8. Its horsepower, torque, and towing ratings remain unchanged: 400 hp at @ 6250 rpm, 410 lb-ft of torque at 4250 rpm, 12,800 pounds.

The final and most significant update to the F-150 for 2027 is the introduction of BlueCruise with Towing, which is exactly what it sounds like: Ford’s hands-free driver assist system now accommodates towing. In very specific conditions, of course: With a trailer of known dimensions, on a pre-qualified divided highway (or “Blue Zone”), at speeds below 75 mph, when said trailer is not exhibiting persistent sway, and the tire pressure monitoring warning light is not on. Also, you’ll need to make any lane changes manually—we know, it’s terribly inconvenient.


We don’t know complete pricing for the 2027 range, but we do know that the two-wheel-drive XL starts at $40,585, including $2795 destination, and that the F-150 Carhartt starts at $62,660… without destination.
